claims.claim: Intratesticular testosterone levels are unchanged in Adgb knockout mice
claims.source: Intratesticular testosterone (Figure 1E) as well as serum luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) remained comparable between wild type and knockouts.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1E showing no significant difference in testosterone levels between wild-type and knockout mice.

claims.claim: Serum LH and FSH levels are unchanged in Adgb knockout mice
claims.source: Intratesticular testosterone (Figure 1E) as well as serum luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) remained comparable between wild type and knockouts.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing no significant difference in LH and FSH levels.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show abnormal spermatogenic maturation with absence of flagella during spermiation
claims.source: In contrast, in knockout animals, despite the presence of meiotic events (stages X–XII, Figure 1F), no flagella could be observed during the spermiation stage (stages VII–VIII, Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Histological examination shown in Figure 1F demonstrates the absence of flagella in knockout animals during spermiation.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice have abnormally shaped sperm heads and trapped stage 16 spermatids
claims.source: The absence of mature sperm was accompanied by abnormally shaped heads, trapped stage 16 spermatids within the epithelium, and the presence of cytoplasmic material filling the lumen of the tubules (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Histological analysis in Figure 1F shows morphological abnormalities in knockout testis sections.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show accumulation of residual bodies and absence of mature sperm in the cauda epididymis
claims.source: Within the cauda epididymis, knockout animals displayed accumulations of residual bodies, cytoplasmic material, shed germ cells, and occasional abnormally shaped sperm heads but an overall absence of mature sperm as compared to wild-type animals (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: Histological examination of epididymis sections shown in Figure 1G demonstrates the absence of mature sperm in knockout animals.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show no increase in oxidative stress markers
claims.source: No differences were detected in knockout testes at mRNA levels of nitric oxide synthases 1–3 (Nos1-3) or superoxide dismutases 1–3 (Sod1-3), the ratio of Bax/Bcl2 was unchanged compared to wild-type testes, and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assays on testis sections revealed no differences, suggesting no increase in oxidative stress or apoptotic events (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: RT-qPCR data and TUNEL assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 demonstrate no significant differences in oxidative stress or apoptosis markers.

claims.claim: Adgb mRNA expression is nearly undetectable until post-natal day 21 and peaks at post-natal day 25
claims.source: Whereas the expression of Adgb remained nearly undetectable until post-natal day 21 (corresponding to the stage of round spermatids), Adgb mRNA levels drastically increased to reach a peak at post-natal day 25, coinciding with the first elongating spermatids (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A demonstrates temporal expression pattern during spermatogenesis.

claims.claim: Adgb protein expression peaks at post-natal days 26-28
claims.source: Accordingly, Adgb protein expression equally reached its peak at post-natal days 26–28, suggesting slightly delayed translation (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B and C demonstrates protein expression levels during development.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show abnormal accumulation of elongating and elongated spermatids
claims.source: While no variations could be detected for phases 2C (spermatogonia, secondary spermatocytes, and testicular somatic cells), S-phase (pre-meiotic spermatogonia), 4C (primary spermatocytes), and 1C (round spermatids), an abnormal accumulation of elongating and elongated spermatids (phase H) could be detected in knockout animals, suggesting a blockade in the elongation process (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2D demonstrates significant accumulation of phase H cells (p=0.00024).

claims.claim: Adgb is expressed in post-meiotic cells and mature sperm
claims.source: Additionally, immunofluorescence (Figure 2E), mRNA in situ hybridization (Figure 2F), and X-gal (Figure 2G) stainings of testis sections from wild-type and knockout mice confirmed the presence of Adgb within layers containing post-meiotic cells and further intensifying toward the lumen and mature sperm (Figure 2E–G).
claims.evidence: Multiple staining techniques shown in Figures 2E-G demonstrate Adgb localization in testis sections.

claims.claim: Adgb is localized to the midpiece and flagellum of mature sperm
claims.source: Moreover, in mature sperm, Adgb expression could be visualized within the midpiece and along the whole flagellum by both X-gal (Figure 2G) and immunofluorescence (Figure 2H) stainings.
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence and X-gal staining shown in Figures 2G and 2H demonstrate subcellular localization in sperm.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout sperm display multiple flagellar malformations including coiled, bifid or shortened flagella
claims.source: While wild-type sperm appeared normal, very few knockout spermatozoa were found and displayed various defects of the head and/or flagellum structure, including shortened or bifid tails, loopings of the flagellum, and immature acrosomal structures (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Microscopic examination shown in Figure 3A demonstrates morphological abnormalities in knockout sperm.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout sperm show various acrosome defects
claims.source: Knockout sperm acrosome structure appeared partially conserved, with sperm displaying either normal acrosomes, or various defects in shape or staining intensity, or total absence (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Peanut agglutinin staining shown in Figure 3B demonstrates acrosome abnormalities in knockout sperm.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show disorganized microtubular structures in sperm flagella
claims.source: Whereas numerous axonemes displaying the regular 9+2 structure from step 9 spermatids could be found in wild types, none were found in knockouts at the same stage. In later stages (step 12 spermatids and onward), rare and abnormal axonemes could be observed in knockouts, displaying disorganized microtubular structures and forming microtubular clusters without defined fibrous or mitochondrial sheath (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: TEM analysis shown in Figure 3C demonstrates ultrastructural defects in axoneme formation.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show misshaped sperm heads with nuclear inclusions
claims.source: We could further observe misshaped heads with nuclear inclusions, defective manchette elongation, and abnormal acrosomes in knockout sections (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: TEM images shown in Figures 3C-F demonstrate multiple structural abnormalities in knockout spermatids.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show defective manchette elongation
claims.source: We could further observe misshaped heads with nuclear inclusions, defective manchette elongation, and abnormal acrosomes in knockout sections (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: TEM analysis shown in Figure 3E demonstrates manchette defects in knockout spermatids.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout results in dysregulation of 278 genes (74 upregulated and 204 downregulated)
claims.source: An elaborate set of significantly differentially expressed genes (74 genes upregulated and 204 downregulated) was identified, underscoring the crucial function of Adgb in spermatogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A identifies differentially expressed genes in knockout testes.

claims.claim: Differentially expressed genes in Adgb knockout mice are enriched for functions related to sperm development and motility
claims.source: Functional analysis based on gene ontology term enrichments confirmed that many of these genes are related to sperm head, acrosome reaction, acrosomal membrane, sperm motility, spermatid development, and spermatid differentiation, in line with the pronounced structural changes in spermatids during spermiogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrates functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes.

claims.claim: Sept10 is enriched in Adgb immunoprecipitation from testis lysates
claims.source: Among the specifically enriched proteins, there were various members of the septin family, such as Sept10, Sept11, Sept2, and Sept7 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 4).
claims.evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis following immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 4A demonstrates Sept10 enrichment.

claims.claim: Adgb and Sept10 interact in vivo in testis lysates
claims.source: The results demonstrate that Adgb and Sept10 interact both in vivo (Figure 4B) and in vitro (Figure 4C), whereas in testis lysates of Adgb-deficient mice, no Sept10 co-precipitation was observed (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4B demonstrate protein-protein interaction in testis lysates.

claims.claim: Adgb and Sept10 interact in vitro in HEK293 cells
claims.source: The results demonstrate that Adgb and Sept10 interact both in vivo (Figure 4B) and in vitro (Figure 4C), whereas in testis lysates of Adgb-deficient mice, no Sept10 co-precipitation was observed (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4C demonstrate protein-protein interaction in transfected cells.

claims.claim: Endogenous Sept10 protein levels are unchanged in Adgb knockout testes
claims.source: Endogenous Sept10 protein levels were equal in testis lysates of Adgb-deficient and wild-type mice, as were endogenous levels of Sept11, Sept7, and Sept2, as well as other septins that are crucial for spermatogenesis, including Sept8, Sept9, and Sept14 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 demonstrates no change in septin protein levels.

claims.claim: Adgb does not interact with Sept2, Sept7, or Sept11 in co-IP experiments
claims.source: Reciprocal co-IP experiments between Adgb and other enriched septins (Sept2, Sept7, and Sept11) revealed no interaction, neither in vivo nor in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), whereas SEPT7 and SEPT10 interacted in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 3 demonstrate lack of interaction with other septins.

claims.claim: Both N-terminal and C-terminal portions of ADGB interact with SEPT10
claims.source: Following co-overexpression of ADGB deletion constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) with SEPT10 and subsequent co-IP, immunoblotting revealed that both parts of ADGB interact with SEPT10 (Figure 4D and E) and that this interaction remained intact also upon deletion of the coiled-coil domain of ADGB (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments with deletion constructs shown in Figures 4D and 4E demonstrate interaction with both protein regions.

claims.claim: The ADGB-SEPT10 interaction is maintained upon deletion of the coiled-coil domain
claims.source: Following co-overexpression of ADGB deletion constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) with SEPT10 and subsequent co-IP, immunoblotting revealed that both parts of ADGB interact with SEPT10 (Figure 4D and E) and that this interaction remained intact also upon deletion of the coiled-coil domain of ADGB (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 demonstrate maintained interaction with coiled-coil deletion mutant.

claims.claim: Adgb and Sept10 co-localize at the sperm annulus in S12 and S15 spermatids and mature sperm
claims.source: Co-localization of Adgb and Sept10 was visible during spermatid maturation and in flagella in testis sections (Figure 5A) and at the level of the sperm annulus in S12 and S15 spermatids and mature wild-type sperm (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrates co-localization of the two proteins.

claims.claim: Sept10 is also localized to the neck region of S15 spermatids and mature sperm
claims.source: A moderate Sept10 staining was also observed in the neck region of S15 spermatids and in mature sperm (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrates Sept10 localization in the neck region.

claims.claim: Sept10 shows abnormal migration in Adgb knockout spermatids and sperm
claims.source: However, in knockout S12 and S15 spermatids, as well as in epididymal sperm, only a single signal, likely corresponding to the annulus as verified by Sept7 staining of epididymal sperm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), was observed and displayed abnormal migration, indicating defective manchette or microtubule formation (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrates mislocalization of Sept10 in knockout cells.

claims.claim: Adgb knockout mice show abnormal mitochondrial organization in spermatids and sperm
claims.source: As expected, a robust staining was observed along the whole midpiece in wild-type spermatids and sperm, whereas mitochondria were barely visible and formed a cloudy structure around the neck region of knockout spermatids and sperm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: CoxIV staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B demonstrates abnormal mitochondrial localization in knockout cells.

claims.claim: Overexpressed ADGB contributes to proteolytic cleavage of overexpressed SEPT10 in HEK293 cells
claims.source: Intriguingly, apart from the intact form of overexpressed SEPT10 at 60 kDa, increased levels of a lower band of 37 kDa were consistently detected in the presence of co-overexpressed ADGB in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A demonstrates dose-dependent appearance of a SEPT10 cleavage product.

claims.claim: The 37 kDa band detected upon ADGB-SEPT10 co-expression is a proteolytic SEPT10 product
claims.source: Immunoblotting with a V5-antibody upon co-overexpression of a C-terminal V5-tagged SEPT10 with ADGB (Figure 6B) as well as the presence of this band upon SEPT10/ADGB co-IP (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) further supports its origin as proteolytic SEPT10 product.
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting with V5-tagged SEPT10 shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 confirms the band is a SEPT10 fragment.

claims.claim: ADGB-dependent SEPT10 cleavage is oxygen-independent
claims.source: To investigate a potential oxygen-dependent influence of the globin domain, this experiment was repeated under normoxic and hypoxic conditions (0.2% O2) but no differences were observed upon exposure to hypoxic conditions (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting under normoxic and hypoxic conditions shown in Figure 6C demonstrates no oxygen-dependence of SEPT10 cleavage.

claims.claim: Deletion of the IQ domain reduces ADGB-dependent SEPT10 cleavage
claims.source: Notably, transient overexpression of IQ-mutant ADGB resulted in considerably reduced appearance of the 37 kDa SEPT10 band relative to wild-type ADGB (Figure 6D), and the same was observed with an ADGB protease domain deletion mutant, further supporting a CaM-dependent proteolytic cleavage (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting with IQ deletion mutant shown in Figure 6D demonstrates reduced SEPT10 cleavage.

claims.claim: Deletion of the protease domain reduces ADGB-dependent SEPT10 cleavage
claims.source: Notably, transient overexpression of IQ-mutant ADGB resulted in considerably reduced appearance of the 37 kDa SEPT10 band relative to wild-type ADGB (Figure 6D), and the same was observed with an ADGB protease domain deletion mutant, further supporting a CaM-dependent proteolytic cleavage (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting with protease domain deletion mutant shown in Figure 6D demonstrates reduced SEPT10 cleavage.

claims.claim: A truncated ADGB construct containing the globin and IQ domains interacts with calmodulin
claims.source: Whereas co-IP experiments following overexpression of full-length ADGB did not interact with CaM under basal experimental conditions in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), a truncated construct covering the globin and IQ domains displayed robust ADGB-CaM interaction (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6E demonstrate interaction between the globin domain construct and CaM.

claims.claim: Calmodulin is enriched in immunoprecipitation of the overexpressed ADGB globin domain
claims.source: Consistently, MS analysis of proteins that were present in the IP of the overexpressed, isolated globin domain revealed a prominent enrichment of endogenous CaM (Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—source data 5).
claims.evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 demonstrates CaM enrichment in globin domain IP.

claims.claim: Mutation of critical heme-binding residues does not alter the ADGB-CaM interaction
claims.source: Importantly, individual or double mutation of the proximal histidine (HisF8) or distal glutamine (GlnE7), critical residues in the globin domain for heme coordination, did not alter the interaction, suggesting that the ADGB-CaM interaction occurs independently of heme incorporation (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments with heme-binding mutants shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 4 demonstrate maintained CaM interaction.

claims.claim: The ADGB-CaM interaction is maintained under heme depletion conditions
claims.source: Consistently, upon heme deprivation, robust interaction was observed between CaM and the isolated intact as well as double mutated (HisF8/GlnE7) globin domain. (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments under heme depletion shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 demonstrate heme-independent CaM interaction.

claims.claim: Mammalian 2-hybrid assays demonstrate interaction between ADGB globin domain and calmodulin
claims.source: These M2H assays were performed in two different cell lines, HEK293 and A375, and revealed up to 7.5-fold increase in luciferase activity upon co-transfection of both chimeric proteins compared to single construct transfections, providing independent evidence that ADGB interacts with CaM.
claims.evidence: Mammalian 2-hybrid assays shown in Figures 6G and 6H demonstrate protein-protein interaction through reporter gene activation.

claims.claim: Full-length ADGB does not interact with CaM in mammalian 2-hybrid assays
claims.source: However, when full-length ADGB was employed in M2H assays with interchanged Gal4 and VP16 domains, no interaction with CaM was observed, corroborating the co-IP data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Mammalian 2-hybrid assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B demonstrate lack of interaction with full-length ADGB.

claims.claim: The ADGB-CaM interaction is oxygen-independent
claims.source: Exposure to hypoxic conditions (0.2% O2) did not alter luciferase activity (Figure 6H, left panel), while luciferase activity of a 5'/3'-hypoxia response element-dependent EPO promoter-driven reporter gene increased (Figure 6H, right panel), suggesting that the ADGB-CaM interaction is O2 independent.
claims.evidence: Mammalian 2-hybrid assays under hypoxic conditions shown in Figure 6H demonstrate oxygen-independent interaction.

claims.claim: Adgb is a chimeric protein containing an N-terminal calpain-like cysteine protease domain, a central permuted functional globin domain interrupted by a potential calmodulin-binding IQ motif, and a large C-terminal tail
claims.source: Adgb is a chimeric protein containing an N-terminal calpain-like cysteine protease domain, followed by an uncharacterized 300 amino acid long region, a central permuted functional globin domain (Bracke et al., 2018), interrupted by a potential calmodulin (CaM)-binding IQ motif, and a large 700 amino acid long C-terminal tail of unknown identity (Hoogewijs et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous structural characterization studies (Bracke et al., 2018; Hoogewijs et al., 2012) describing the domain structure.

claims.claim: Decreased ADGB mRNA expression levels are observed in infertile vs. fertile men
claims.source: Decreased mRNA expression levels in infertile vs. fertile men (Platts et al., 2007) suggest a potential role of Adgb in spermatogenesis.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Platts et al., 2007) showing differential expression in human infertility.

claims.claim: Gene regulation and expression studies suggest an association of Adgb with ciliogenesis including flagellum formation
claims.source: Gene regulation and expression studies further suggest an association of Adgb with ciliogenesis including flagellum formation (Koay et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Koay et al., 2021) demonstrating association with ciliogenesis.

claims.claim: Adgb is predominantly expressed in mammalian testis tissue
claims.source: The predominant expression of the latest globin family member, androglobin (Adgb), in mammalian testis tissue prompted us to assess its physiological function in spermatogenesis.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about Adgb expression pattern.

claims.claim: Spermatogenesis is a complex differentiation process ending with production of mature haploid spermatozoa
claims.source: Spermatogenesis is a complex and dynamic differentiation process ending by the production of mature haploid spermatozoa (Hermo et al., 2010a; Hermo et al., 2010b; Hermo et al., 2010c; Hermo et al., 2010d; Hermo et al., 2010e).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references (Hermo et al., 2010a-e) describing the spermatogenesis process.

claims.claim: Over 4000 genes are possibly implicated in spermatogenesis
claims.source: it is believed that over 4000 genes are possibly implicated in spermatogenesis (Jan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Jan et al., 2017) estimating the number of genes involved in spermatogenesis.

claims.claim: Sperm defects and abnormalities remain idiopathic in about 30% of cases
claims.source: It is currently estimated that sperm defects and abnormalities remain idiopathic in about 30% of cases (Fainberg and Kashanian, 2019; Tüttelmann et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Fainberg and Kashanian, 2019; Tüttelmann et al., 2018) providing epidemiological data on idiopathic male infertility.

claims.claim: Calmodulin is one of the most conserved proteins in eukaryotes and serves as a secondary messenger
claims.source: CaM is one of the most conserved proteins in eukaryotes and serves as a secondary messenger following intracellular binding of Ca2+ and interaction with one of the more than 300 identified downstream target proteins (Andrews et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Andrews et al., 2020) describing calmodulin function and conservation.

claims.claim: Calmodulin participates in spermatogenesis and sperm maturation and function
claims.source: CaM is the main intracellular receptor for Ca2+, thereby participating in almost every biological process, including spermatogenesis and sperm maturation and function (Darszon et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Darszon et al., 2011) describing calmodulin's role in spermatogenesis.

claims.claim: Septins are conserved GTPases that form oligomers and filamentous polymers
claims.source: Septins are conserved GTPases that have the ability to form large oligomers and filamentous polymers and which associate with cell membranes and with the cytoskeleton. They serve as scaffolds for the proper localization of intracellular proteins via their diffusion barrier-forming characteristics (Dolat et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Dolat et al., 2014) describing septin structure and function.

claims.claim: Various septins localize to the sperm annulus where they form the septin ring
claims.source: In sperm, various septins (including Sept1, Sept4, Sept6, Sept7, and Sept12) have been localized to the sperm annulus, where they polymerize to a filamentous structure called the septin ring, forming a barrier between the midpiece and the principal piece of the spermatozoon (Toure et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Toure et al., 2011) describing septin localization and function in sperm.

claims.claim: Sept4 knockout mice are infertile and display disorganized sperm mitochondria
claims.source: Supportive of this function, Sept4-/- and Sept12+/- mice are infertile and display disorganized sperm mitochondria (Ihara et al., 2005; Kissel et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Ihara et al., 2005; Kissel et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2009) describing phenotypes of septin knockout mice.

claims.claim: Sept4 knockout mice display a bent sperm tail and absence of annulus
claims.source: Moreover, Sept4-/- mice display a bent sperm tail and absence of annulus (Ihara et al., 2005; Kissel et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Ihara et al., 2005; Kissel et al., 2005) describing Sept4 knockout phenotypes.

claims.claim: Sept12 heterozygous mice exhibit broken acrosomes, misshaped nuclei, and increased apoptosis of germ cells
claims.source: whereas Sept12+/- mice exhibit broken acrosomes, misshaped nuclei, and increased apoptosis of germ cells (Lin et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Lin et al., 2009) describing Sept12 heterozygous mouse phenotypes.

claims.claim: SEPT12 mutations have been described in infertile men displaying abnormal sperm
claims.source: Correspondingly, SEPT12 mutations have been described in infertile men displaying abnormal sperm including defective annulus with a bent tail (Kuo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Kuo et al., 2012) describing SEPT12 mutations in human infertility.

claims.claim: SEPT14 missense mutations are associated with defective sperm head morphology and DNA integrity
claims.source: Additionally, defective sperm head morphology and DNA integrity have recently been reported for two different SEPT14 missense mutations (Lin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Lin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019) describing SEPT14 mutations and associated phenotypes.

claims.claim: Sept12 mutations disrupt the septin complex at the sperm neck and lead to loss of Sept10 signal in the annulus
claims.source: Two mutations of Sept12 identified in patients disrupted the complex, leading to unstable head-tail junctions and defective connecting piece formation. Strikingly, the mutation of Sept12 and the subsequent disruption of the complex led to loss of Sept10 signal in the annulus (Shen et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Shen et al., 2020) describing Sept12 mutations and their effects on Sept10 localization.

claims.claim: Sept2 forms a diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium
claims.source: Sept2 forms a diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium, impeding ciliary formation through loss of Sonic Hedgehog signaling when depleted (Hu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Hu et al., 2010) describing Sept2 function in cilia.

claims.claim: Sept2/7/9 form a complex that associates with the ciliary axoneme and regulates ciliary length
claims.source: Sept2/7/9 form a complex that associates with the ciliary axoneme, thereby regulating ciliary length (Ghossoub et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Ghossoub et al., 2013) describing septin complex function in cilia.

claims.claim: Most ciliopathies include male infertility and immotile sperm due to defective axonemal organization
claims.source: Furthermore, most ciliopathies include male infertility and immotile sperm due to defective axonemal organization (Brown and Witman, 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Brown and Witman, 2014) describing ciliopathies and male infertility.

claims.claim: Adgb is consistently present in the ciliomes of three distinct evolutionary ancestral taxa
claims.source: Moreover, a recent study reported the consistent presence of Adgb in the ciliomes of three distinct evolutionary ancestral taxa, further suggesting a conserved function related to microtubular organization and likely flagella formation (Sigg et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Sigg et al., 2017) demonstrating Adgb presence in ciliomes across taxa.

claims.claim: Adgb is transcriptionally regulated by FoxJ1, a master regulator of ciliogenesis
claims.source: In line with this study, our recent in vitro investigations have demonstrated that Adgb is transcriptionally regulated by FoxJ1, a master regulator of ciliogenesis (Koay et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Koay et al., 2021) demonstrating transcriptional regulation of Adgb by FoxJ1.

claims.claim: Calpain-dependent proteolytic cleavage of Sept5 triggers secretion of chemokine-containing granules in platelets
claims.source: Calpain-dependent proteolytic cleavage of septins is not unprecedented; it was shown that Sept5 is a substrate of both calpain-1 and calpain-2 in platelets, where the cleavage triggers secretion of chemokine-containing granules (Randriamboavonjy et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Randriamboavonjy et al., 2012) describing calpain-mediated septin cleavage.

claims.claim: SUMOylation impacts Sept6, 7, and 11-dependent filament formation
claims.source: Septins are sensitive to molecular modifications, such as SUMOylation which impacts Sept6, 7, and 11-dependent filament formation (Ribet et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Ribet et al., 2017) describing SUMOylation effects on septin filaments.

claims.claim: PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Sept12 leads to its dissociation from the septin complex
claims.source: or to PKA-dependent phosphorylation as reported for Sept12, leading to its dissociation from the septin complex and disruption of filament formation (Shen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study (Shen et al., 2017) describing phosphorylation effects on Sept12.

claims.claim: The Adgbtm1a(KOMP)Wtsi allele was generated by blastocyst microinjection of ESC clone EPD0707_3_H06
claims.source: The Adgbtm1a(KOMP)Wtsi (tm1a) strain was generated by blastocyst microinjection of ESC clone EPD0707_3_H06, provided by the KOMP (Skarnes et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to generate the knockout mouse line and cites the KOMP resource (Skarnes et al., 2011).

claims.claim: No significant differences in Mendelian distribution of offspring were observed for Adgb tm1d animals
claims.source: Genotyping was performed by regular PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and revealed no significant differences in the Mendelian distribution of offspring for Adgb tm1d animals following interbreeding of heterozygous parents (380 pups: +/+, n=101; +/-, n=168; -/-, n=111; Χ2=5.62, p>0.05, ns).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents genotyping data with statistical analysis showing normal Mendelian ratios.

claims.claim: Full penetrance male infertility was observed in homozygous tm1a and tm1b male mice
claims.source: Full penetrance male infertility was also observed in homozygous tm1a and tm1b male mice, whereas homozygous tm1c animals showed normal fertility (data not shown).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observations from breeding experiments with different alleles.

claims.claim: Homozygous tm1c animals showed normal fertility
claims.source: Full penetrance male infertility was also observed in homozygous tm1a and tm1b male mice, whereas homozygous tm1c animals showed normal fertility (data not shown).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports observations from breeding experiments showing that the conditional allele does not affect fertility.

claims.claim: Adgb is required for male fertility
claims.source: Androglobin, a chimeric mammalian globin, is required for male fertility
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the title and supported by the complete infertility phenotype of male knockout mice.

claims.claim: Adgb is essential for murine spermatogenesis
claims.source: Collectively, our results provide evidence that Adgb is essential for murine spermatogenesis and further suggest that Adgb is required for sperm head shaping via the manchette and proper flagellum formation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the multiple phenotypes observed in knockout mice.

claims.claim: Adgb is required for sperm head shaping via the manchette
claims.source: Collectively, our results provide evidence that Adgb is essential for murine spermatogenesis and further suggest that Adgb is required for sperm head shaping via the manchette and proper flagellum formation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observed manchette defects and abnormal head morphology in knockout mice.

claims.claim: Adgb is required for proper flagellum formation
claims.source: Collectively, our results provide evidence that Adgb is essential for murine spermatogenesis and further suggest that Adgb is required for sperm head shaping via the manchette and proper flagellum formation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the multiple flagellar defects observed in knockout mice.

claims.claim: The absence of Adgb leads to mislocalization of Sept10 in sperm
claims.source: Furthermore, the absence of Adgb leads to mislocalization of Sept10 in sperm, indicating defective manchette and sperm annulus formation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on immunofluorescence data showing abnormal Sept10 localization in knockout sperm.

claims.claim: In vitro data suggest that Adgb contributes to Sept10 proteolysis in a calmodulin-dependent manner
claims.source: Finally, in vitro data suggest that Adgb contributes to Sept10 proteolysis in a calmodulin-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on in vitro experiments showing SEPT10 cleavage that is reduced by IQ domain deletion.

claims.claim: The observed male infertility could be the result of defects in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis

results.result: Adgb knockout mice display complete male infertility with reduced testis weight, while female fertility and hormonal signaling remain normal. The infertility phenotype shows full penetrance in tm1a, tm1b, and tm1d alleles but not in the conditional tm1c allele, and Mendelian ratios are maintained.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C70-C73 collectively demonstrate male infertility with appropriate controls. The breeding data (C1, C71), testis weight measurements (C2), normal hormone levels (C3, C4), and genetic validation (C70-C72) provide converging evidence. The conditional allele control (C72) strengthens the conclusion that the phenotype is specifically due to Adgb loss.

results.result: Adgb knockout mice exhibit severe defects in spermiogenesis including absence of flagella during spermiation, abnormally shaped sperm heads, trapped spermatids, disorganized microtubular structures, defective manchette elongation, and various acrosome defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C14-C18 are supported by multiple complementary techniques including histology (C5-C7), light microscopy (C14-C15), and TEM (C16-C18). The convergence of evidence from different methodological approaches at multiple stages of spermatogenesis provides strong support for these structural defects.

results.result: Adgb knockout mice show no increase in oxidative stress or apoptotic markers in testes.
results.evaluation: Claim C8 is supported by multiple independent measurements including RT-qPCR for Nos1-3, Sod1-3, Bax/Bcl2 ratio, and TUNEL assays. These complementary approaches consistently show no differences between wild-type and knockout mice, ruling out oxidative stress or increased apoptosis as primary mechanisms.

results.result: Adgb expression is temporally regulated during spermatogenesis, with mRNA peaking at post-natal day 25 and protein at days 26-28, coinciding with elongating spermatids. Adgb localizes to post-meiotic cells, the sperm midpiece, and flagellum, with knockout mice showing abnormal accumulation of elongating spermatids.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 are supported by RT-qPCR (C9), immunoblotting (C10), flow cytometry (C11), and multiple localization techniques including immunofluorescence, in situ hybridization, and X-gal staining (C12-C13). The temporal and spatial expression patterns are internally consistent and align with the observed phenotypes.

results.result: Adgb knockout results in dysregulation of 278 genes (74 upregulated, 204 downregulated) enriched for functions related to sperm development, motility, and spermiogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by RNAseq analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds and gene ontology enrichment analysis. The functional enrichment for spermatogenesis-related genes is consistent with the observed phenotypes. However, the manuscript does not provide validation of individual differentially expressed genes by independent methods.

results.result: Sept10 is specifically enriched in Adgb immunoprecipitation and interacts with Adgb both in vivo (testis lysates) and in vitro (HEK293 cells), while other septins (Sept2, Sept7, Sept11) do not interact with Adgb. Endogenous septin protein levels remain unchanged in knockout testes.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are supported by mass spectrometry (C21), reciprocal co-IP experiments in both testis lysates and cell culture (C22-C23, C25), and immunoblotting (C24). The specificity of the Adgb-Sept10 interaction is demonstrated by negative results with other septins, and the lack of change in septin levels rules out indirect effects through protein stability.

results.result: Both N-terminal and C-terminal portions of ADGB interact with SEPT10, and this interaction is maintained upon deletion of the coiled-coil domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by co-IP experiments with deletion constructs shown in Figures 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5. The demonstration that both protein regions interact suggests multiple interaction surfaces, though the biological significance of this redundancy is not explored.

results.result: Adgb and Sept10 co-localize at the sperm annulus in S12 and S15 spermatids and mature sperm, with Sept10 also present in the neck region. In knockout mice, Sept10 shows abnormal migration and mitochondria display disorganized localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by immunofluorescence data in testis sections, microdissected tubules, and epididymal sperm (Figures 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B). The co-localization in wild-type and mislocalization in knockout mice provide functional evidence linking Adgb to Sept10 positioning and mitochondrial organization.

results.result: Overexpressed ADGB contributes to proteolytic cleavage of overexpressed SEPT10 in HEK293 cells in a dose-dependent, oxygen-independent manner that requires both the IQ domain and protease domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by immunoblotting experiments showing dose-dependent cleavage (C32), V5-tagging confirmation (C33), hypoxia experiments (C34), and deletion mutant analysis (C35-C36). The convergence of evidence from multiple experimental approaches supports the conclusion, though the physiological relevance of this in vitro observation requires further validation.

results.result: A truncated ADGB construct containing the globin and IQ domains interacts with calmodulin in a heme-independent and oxygen-independent manner, while full-length ADGB does not interact with CaM under basal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 are supported by co-IP experiments (C37, C39-C40), mass spectrometry (C38), mammalian 2-hybrid assays (C41-C43), and experiments with heme-binding mutants and heme depletion (C39-C40). The multiple independent approaches and controls for heme and oxygen dependence provide strong support, though the lack of interaction with full-length ADGB raises questions about physiological relevance.

results.result: The Adgbtm1a(KOMP)Wtsi allele was generated by blastocyst microinjection of ESC clone EPD0707_3_H06.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by the description of the gene targeting strategy with appropriate citation of the KOMP resource and validation by PCR and Southern blotting as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Adgb is essential for murine spermatogenesis and is required for sperm head shaping via the manchette, proper flagellum formation, and Sept10 localization. In vitro data suggest Adgb contributes to Sept10 proteolysis in a calmodulin-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental data. These are well-supported by the convergence of in vivo phenotypic data (C1-C18, C28-C31) and in vitro mechanistic studies (C32-C43). However, the mechanistic link between the in vitro SEPT10 cleavage and the in vivo phenotypes remains inferential.

results.result: The male infertility phenotype represents direct effects of Adgb deficiency in testis rather than defects in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, as evidenced by unchanged LH, FSH, and testosterone levels, though indirect effects cannot be entirely excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide appropriate consideration of alternative mechanisms. The hormone measurements (C3-C4) support the conclusion of direct testicular effects (C80-C81), while the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C82). The inference connecting testosterone levels to Adgb expression patterns (C83) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: The data suggest an interdependence between Adgb and Sept10 required for annulus maintenance, with potential scaffolding and regulatory functions. The ADGB-SEPT10 interaction may serve as a targeting mechanism for proteolytic processing, possibly involving liberation of the globin domain by proteolytic cleavage.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 and C93 are largely speculative interpretations (marked as SPECULATION or INFERENCE in evidence_type) that extend beyond the direct experimental evidence. While these hypotheses are reasonable given the data, they require additional experimental validation including in vivo demonstration of SEPT10 cleavage, identification of the protease responsible, and functional rescue experiments.

results.result: Time-dependent truncation of ADGB occurs in both insect cells and HEK293 cells, consistent with the autolytic nature of Ca2+-dependent calpains.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by previous observations in insect cells (C90, citation), current observations in HEK293 cells (C91), and established knowledge about calpain auto-proteolysis (C92, citations). This provides context for the proposed mechanism, though direct demonstration of auto-proteolysis is not provided.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about Adgb structure, expression patterns, spermatogenesis, calmodulin, septins, and their roles in male fertility based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C68, C84, and C92 represent background knowledge and prior work appropriately cited from the literature. These provide essential context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field.
